text: Mr. Mayor, members of council, as we've done in the past with our COVID related updates, we've grouped them together for sake of ease of discussion. Okay, and we'll go to the first slide. As the report notes, we continue to have the lowest prevalence of positive cases in Northern Ontario, and Northern Ontario itself is far lower than most areas in Southern Ontario. That's really good news for us. The community continues to respond well to complying with both provincial orders and Algoma public health recommendations. However, this will be more challenging as we enter the later spring and summer as people quite frankly are social creatures and with the good weather, they want to be more active and they are, it has been challenging being locked in there, not a total lockdown, but having restrictions on their activities. As the mayor noted though, it's important to keep complying with recommendations and that is the wearing of face masks if you can't physically distance and the need to physically distance and to keep our interactions with others to a minimum as possible. We do know that there is a community spread out there in our community that isn't tracked. We have had some of our positive cases that we can't pin down where they had the contact and they caught it. So we need to keep our guard up and we can't be complacent in dealing with these measures. For the corporation itself, our public closures are continued, but there are starting to be limited reopening of some facilities and services. As we do this, our reopening is guided by provincial orders which allow us to reopen certain things, but we have operational constraints. We have to assess the community need and we know that the desire by the community for services needs to be balanced off with what our current operational constraints are. And we also have to keep an eye for community health and look at our facilities and assess how we can monitor their use and how we can monitor the community abiding by the recommendations of Algoma Public Health. The services reopening now include our marina, just the Bellevue Marina for now, that is our residential marina, not the transient marina at Bonder. Also our tennis and pickleball courts, pump track, skateboard park, off leash dog area and disc golf. And reopening soon at the end of this week would be ball diamonds and soccer fields for casual use only. There can be no team play. Anyone using them still needs to observe physical distancing unless they are a family unit, of course, and since they live together, they can be a little closer together and do the activity. The staff implications and all of this, we have started to recall some of our laid off staff as we've had to address opening some of these areas. The redeployment that we have done does continue in some areas, but we are returning some redeployed staff to regular duties than others. We are returning some of our staff who have been working remotely to the workplace in stages so that we can prepare for limited public interaction as we move towards further reopening measures. We do also have to reeducate these staff, many of who have been absent working remotely for the entire pandemic, to new workplace health and safety measures that we have in our various work sites, including the Civic Center, and that means being able to physically distance from each other, staff, as we do our job, and increased cleaning protocols and things to watch for. Summer student employment is underway, but as mentioned before, it will be at a reduced level this year. As the CFO Treasurer's report on financial impacts to the end of May reports, the net operating budget impact is 996,740. This is a lower number than frankly staff expected, but as we add everything up, this is where we sit. So that is, while it is a large number, it is a bit of good news for us in that it wasn't greater than that. I would note from the report, where it talks about interim taxes, what you see as a budget impact right now is what we forego in interest and penalty revenue that we would normally get. The report does note that the interim taxes that weren't paid this year is essentially double from what we saw in 2019, but it also notes that three quarters of that increase is limited to 50 non-residential accounts. Really what we see when we see that pattern, we have 50 non-residential accounts that are still outstanding, and that can basically be summed up in three streams. One, there will be commercial and industrial accounts that can't pay right now. So they are withholding the taxes, but they will come later. Two, there will be businesses that can pay, but they wish to preserve their liquidity right now. We're all unsure of how long this will go, so they choose to take the measures that Council has given them by waiving the interest and penalties, and they're preserving their liquidity for now. The third element will be businesses that could pay right now, but they choose not to because like a good business owner, they will not pay until they have to. We need to do a little more work on analyzing how many of those fall into the various groups, but it is important to note that the CFO notes in her report we will work in the end with individual accounts that cannot pay to come up with plans of how they can pay us over time. The report also notes that the reserves contribution impact is a negative 146,000 so far, and most of that is to do with the revenue received from the Municipal Accommodations Tax. The report does note that this is fine for the operations in tourism, that we are fine and still operating with what we've received in. What you will see impacted is money that would be put towards reserves and used in the Tourism Development Fund. So we will see an impact on there. It's also important to note that the interest being waived on the Municipal Accommodations Tax and our accounts receivable aside from taxes does expire at the end of June. So you can expect a report coming to you in June as to whether we should extend that or not. The report also notes our capital funding impact so far is estimated at $2 million, and that is as a result of waiving the sewer surcharge for those two months. It's important to note that the waiving of that money and the reduction in going towards the sewer surcharge capital account will be dealt with near the end with short-term borrowing in the end once we get to building the facilities that are needed and we see what kind of tender pricing is in there. We had always determined that there would be a certain amount of short-term borrowing needed for those projects. So this will just increase that need potentially once we get down the road. Over to our last slide. I had reported on capital projects to you at the previous meeting. As you know, the 2020 resurfacing program is on tonight. We are preparing for anticipated stimulus funding. We've got those, there's preparations underway and a report will come to you for the next meeting that is a typo, it's June 8th, our next council meeting.
